title: One-Mind Undisturbed
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The Buddha Speaks of the Amitabha Sūtra is the essential teaching that the World-Honored One proclaimed of his own accord, without being asked — the profound sūtra praised by the Buddhas of all directions, the wondrous Dharma of ultimate expedient means, the supreme and perfect guide. Within it, the World-Honored One specifically revealed the way to ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss: with sincere faith and vows, uphold the Name in one mind undisturbed. Thereby he established the fundamental teaching of the Pure Land school.

inline.s: The Buddha Speaks of the Amitabha Sūtra is the essential teaching that the World-Honored One proclaimed of his own accord, without being asked — the profound sūtra praised by the Buddhas of all directions, the wondrous Dharma of ultimate expedient means, the supreme and perfect guide. Within it, the World-Honored One specifically revealed the way to ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss: with sincere faith and vows, uphold the Name in one mind undisturbed. Thereby he established the fundamental teaching of the Pure Land school.
In the Buddha Speaks of the Amitabha Sūtra, the World-Honored One said:

“Śāriputra! If there is any good man or good woman who hears the name of Amitabha Buddha and holds fast to that name — for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days — with one mind undisturbed, then at the hour of death that person will see Amitabha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy ones, appear before them. At the end of life their mind will not be inverted, and they shall at once be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitabha Buddha.”

Master Ouyi (Zhixu), the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school, says in his Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra: “This sūtra takes faith, vows, and the recitation of the name as the essential path of practice. Without faith, the vows cannot be awakened; without vows, practice cannot be guided; without the wondrous practice of upholding the Name, the vow cannot be fulfilled and the faith cannot be realized. The sūtra first sets forth the adorned land and its Lord to give rise to faith; then it encourages the making of vows to guide practice; then it reveals the recitation of the name as the direct path to the stage of non-retrogression. Faith means faith in oneself and in another, faith in the cause and in the effect, faith in the phenomenal and in the noumenal. Vows mean to be weary of the Sahā world and to long for the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Practice means to uphold the Name, with one mind undisturbed.” (See
Annotated Commentary on the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sūtra
for the full text.)

Faith and vows must be embodied in diligent recitation of the Buddha’s name before they can be called genuine faith and earnest vows. Reading Master Ouyi’s two statements together — “without the wondrous practice of upholding the Name, the vow cannot be fulfilled and the faith cannot be realized” and “practice means to uphold the Name, with one mind undisturbed” — their concrete meaning is this: without the one-mind-undisturbed practice of upholding the Name, one can neither fulfill the vow nor realize the faith. So the grounding and the concrete expression of genuine faith and earnest vows lie in that one-mind-undisturbed practice of upholding the Name.

Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, says: “One-mind undisturbed is the final refuge of the pure karma of rebirth, the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, one is never secure. How can those who study the Dharma fail to strive for it!” (The Spoken Words of Master Chewu)
In Master Xuanzang’s translation of the Amitabha Sūtra, the Sūtra of Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Reception, the Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! If any good man or good woman of pure faith, having heard of this name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, with its immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable meritorious virtues, and of the adorned virtue of the Land of Ultimate Bliss — having heard it, reflects upon it for one day and one night, or for two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven days, with thought collected and undisturbed — then that good man or good woman, at the end of life, will be surrounded before and behind by the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, together with his immeasurable śrāvaka disciples and the assembly of bodhisattvas, who come to stand before them and, with compassionate protection and blessing, keep their mind from confusion. Having surrendered the life, they will follow the Buddha’s assembly and be born in that pure Buddha-land, the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life. Again, Śāriputra! I contemplate this great matter of benefit and peace and speak these truthful words: if any good man or good woman of pure faith hears this name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, with its inconceivable meritorious virtues, and of that pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all believe, accept, and vow, and, practicing as taught, be born in that Buddha-land.”
(See
Annotated Commentary on the Sūtra of Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Reception
for the full text.)
Please pay special attention:
“They should all believe, accept, and vow, and, practicing as taught, be born in that Buddha-land.”

To seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must have genuine faith, earnest vows, and actual practice. Faith, vows, and practice stand together like the three legs of a tripod — none can be lacking. Faith is the eye and the guide, vows are the motive power, and practice is the carrying-out, the concrete embodiment of faith and vows. The Jing Zhong Jing You Jing (The Path within the Path) says: “If faith is already sincere and vows already firm, yet there is no actual practice to spur oneself on, then faith is but vain faith and vows but vain vows. Empty words avail nothing; how could one hope to gain [rebirth]? In every undertaking one must endure bitter toil before it can be accomplished — how much more so in the great matter of transcending this world!” Therefore we students of the Pure Land should, through the actual practice of one-mind undisturbed, realize our genuine faith and fulfill our earnest vows.
The reason Buddha-recitation must be one-mind is that
only through a Pure Land in the mind is one reborn in the Western Pure Land; through the pure mind of Buddha-recitation one is drawn to be reborn in that Western Pure Land
Master Yinguang says:

“Only where there is a Pure Land in the mind can one be reborn in the Western Pure Land. If one’s own mind is not pure, how could one be reborn there at once? Even the most rebellious and wicked, guilty of the gravest offenses, who are reborn by ten recitations of the Buddha’s name, are reborn because through the pure mind of Buddha-recitation they are drawn to that Western Pure Land.”
(In the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Answering Twenty-Seven Questions from Layman Qu Tianxiang.)
As for why these ten recitations at the moment of death bring rebirth, Master Yinguang explains:
“Apart from this recitation there is absolutely no other thought. Although one has not personally realized one-mind undisturbed, in the end one’s mind is entirely free of any differing thought.”
(In the Third Compilation of the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Vol. Two
Letter in Reply to Layman Chen Xinru.)
The original text of this teaching by Master Yinguang is:

“In the Contemplation Sūtra, a person guilty of the five gravest offenses and the ten evil acts, about to die, with the signs of hell appearing before them — if a good teacher (original note: it does not matter whether this is monk or layperson, man or woman; whoever can teach such a person to recite the Buddha’s name is called a good teacher) teaches them to recite the Buddha’s name, be it only ten recitations, or even fewer than ten, and they then die — they too may rely on the Buddha’s compassionate power and be reborn while still carrying their karma. These ten recitations, compared with the ten recitations of ordinary times, have a force far apart as heaven from earth, and so they are reborn. For, pressed by the most extreme suffering of hell, the moment they hear the Buddha’s name they use their whole spirit to recite it. Apart from this recitation there is absolutely no other thought. Although they have not personally realized one-mind undisturbed, in the end their mind is entirely free of any differing thought.”
Master Yinguang further says:

“To recite the Buddha’s name with a scattered mind rarely brings rebirth. This method can bring the mind back to a single focus; reciting the Buddha’s name with one mind, one will certainly be reborn.”
(In the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou.)
Master Lianchi says:

“Now that one is one-mind undisturbed, within, the right thought is gathered and fixed; without, one is met and welcomed by the Buddha. Leaving this karmic body behind, one is at last reborn in that land.”
(Commentary on the Amitabha Sūtra)
Please pay special attention: “
Within, the right thought is gathered and fixed; without, the Buddha comes to welcome.
” — This is precisely the principle of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the hour of death!
Question: What is one-mind undisturbed?
Answer: Setting the two translations of the Amitabha Sūtra side by side — Master Kumārajīva’s translation says:
“If for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days, one-mind undisturbed.”
Master Xuanzang’s translation says:
“If for one day and night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven, with thought collected and undisturbed.”

From this we know that “one-mind undisturbed” is the same as “with thought collected and undisturbed.” Thus we see that when Master Kumārajīva translated it as “one-mind undisturbed,” he meant: to recite the Buddha’s name with one intent and undivided attention, not to be disturbed by affliction, bright and distinct, neither drowsy nor scattered. This is what is spoken of in the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Buddha-Recitation by Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, and what Master Shandao calls
“gathering in the six sense faculties with pure thoughts succeeding one another”
, and what Master Shandao says:
“thought following thought in continuity”
Question: When you say “bright and distinct,” do you mean that the Buddha’s name should be recited clearly and distinctly?
Answer: That is not what is meant. “Bright and distinct” means that the name being recited should be bright and distinct within the mind. Zhang Guangwei says:

“In the past I only recited the Buddha’s name in a muddled way. Only now do I know that each character must issue from the heart, and each character must return into the heart. When reciting, first close the eyes and sit upright, gather the spirit and still the thoughts; there must not be the slightest scattered, restless, or drowsy mind. When you open the mouth and sound the name, be sure that the sound issues from the heart and is borne by the mouth; let the breath be attuned and the voice gentle, neither too slow nor too fast. Each character is clear, each phrase follows continuously. Taken apart, a single character may form a phrase; strung together, a hundred or a thousand phrases become just one phrase. It flows on, fine and unbroken, from one sound to ten thousand sounds, from one moment to all twelve hours — without break, without pause, without omission, without lapse. In time, when it is mature and mastered, the flower opens and one sees the Buddha; then, when the moment comes, you will verify it for yourself. It will never deceive anyone.... I wish to tell this to all who recite the Buddha’s name. Know that you must recite with the mind, not merely with the mouth. When you enter this gate, the Buddha is not far away.”
(Surplus Words on the Pure Land)
Question: What does “neither drowsy nor scattered” mean?

Answer: “Neither drowsy nor scattered” means: not drowsy, not scattered. That is to say: if a deluded thought arises, be aware of it and do not follow it, so that one is not disturbed by deluded thoughts. Therefore, one-mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation does not mean that not a single deluded thought arises; it means that one is not blinded and carried away by deluded thoughts (not drowsy), and does not let deluded thoughts run on into trains of thought (not scattered). In short, one is not disturbed by deluded thoughts. Of course, this is only the most elementary requirement of one-mind undisturbed; advancing further upon this foundation, one reaches the state where thought after thought is free of delusion and the Buddha’s name forms a pure, unbroken field.
Question: What are the one-mind of practice and the one-mind of principle?

Answer: Their full names are the one-mind-undisturbed of practice and the one-mind-undisturbed of principle. The one-mind undisturbed spoken of above is the one-mind-undisturbed of practice, attained through upholding the Name and reciting the Buddha. The one-mind-undisturbed of principle is seeing the nature and realizing the mind, attained through cultivating the samādhi of Buddha-recitation. Master Ouyi says:
“The one-mind of practice is the bright and distinct, neither drowsy nor scattered; the one-mind of principle is silently according with the unborn and clearly comprehending one’s own nature.”
(The Collected Treatises of Master Lingfeng · Occasional Talks in the Brahma Chamber)
Question: The sūtra says:
“If for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days, one-mind undisturbed.”
Within a single day, or even within seven days, can one truly attain one-mind undisturbed?

Answer: “For one day, or even for seven days” is an illustrative way of speaking, a phrase with omitted details. The fuller account is what the World-Honored One says in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sūtra (The Greater Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness):
“Monks! Whoever practices the four foundations of mindfulness in this way, correctly,
for seven years
, may expect one of two fruits: the most excellent wisdom here and now
(attaining the fruit of arhatship)
, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-return
(attaining the fruit of anāgāmin)
. Monks!
Say nothing of seven years
Monks!
Say nothing of six years
Monks!
Say nothing of one year
Monks!
Say nothing of seven months
Monks!
Say nothing of one month
Monks!
Say nothing of half a month
, if anyone practices the four foundations of mindfulness in this way, correctly
for seven days
, they may expect one of two fruits: the most excellent wisdom here and now, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-return.”

[The Four Fruits] In cultivating the Four Noble Truths there are four fruits: the fruit of stream-enterer (sotāpanna), the fruit of once-returner (sakadāgāmin), the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin), and the fruit of arhat. Among these, the fourth fruit, arhatship, is the highest; one who attains it is freed from birth and death and no longer takes on a future existence.

As for the question, “Within a single day, or even within seven days, can one truly attain one-mind undisturbed?” — the answer is this: one-mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation is the state of “the ten thousand thoughts returning to the One,” and this returning of the ten thousand thoughts to the One is itself only the most elementary stage of practice. From the standpoint of Chan, one must pass through “the ten thousand thoughts returning to the One” and then “the One returning to Nothing” to see the nature and realize the mind; this is only the first gate of the three gates of Chan (the initial breakthrough, pò běncān), and afterward one must still break through the second gate (chóngguān) and the final gate (láoguān). Therefore some Chan practitioners have already brought the ten thousand thoughts to the One, yet are still quite far from seeing the nature and realizing the mind; but once they hear of the supreme excellence of the Pure Land method and turn to Buddha-recitation, they can attain one-mind undisturbed within a single day, or even within seven days. From ancient times to the present such instances are too numerous to list — see the Record of Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land. And those Chan practitioners who have already seen the nature and realized the mind, when they turn to cultivating the Pure Land method, can attain one-mind undisturbed within a single day; many of them later became patriarchs and great teachers of the Pure Land school — again see the Record of Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land. As for those who have not yet brought the ten thousand thoughts to the One, the time will be somewhat longer; precisely how long depends on each person’s foundation and progress in study and practice. In general, so long as the method is correct (for example, by cultivating in accordance with
Awareness Buddha-Recitation

), then through earnest, diligent effort everyone can attain one-mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation. This requires self-confidence (deep faith that one can attain one-mind undisturbed), perseverance, and determination. That self-confidence, perseverance, and determination can transform one’s destiny is shown by the excellent example of Yu Jingyi, whose story is told in
The Record of Yu Jingyi’s Meeting with the Kitchen God (the original text together with its plain-language rendering)
(for its annotations, see
The Annotated Commentary on the Record of Yu Jingyi’s Meeting with the Kitchen God

Therefore, those who recite the Buddha’s name must have genuine faith and earnest vows and strive diligently without pause. Although a lifetime of toil passes in but a moment, once you reach the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss your life will be immeasurable, your joy without bounds, and you will attain Buddhahood and liberate sentient beings, fulfilling the great bodhi vow.

Question: Some say: “'One-mind undisturbed' means 'reciting the Buddha with a concentrated mind, without mixing or scattering.' 'One-mind' means concentrated, and 'not-scattered' means not mixing, not practicing various practices together.” Is this explanation of “one-mind undisturbed” correct?

Answer: This explanation is quite mistaken. As for what is called “one-mind undisturbed,” the Buddha Speaks of the Amitabha Sūtra clearly states: uphold the Name, with one mind undisturbed. That is to say, while holding fast to the name, the thoughts are concentrated and not scattered. So “not-scattered” means that, while holding fast to the name, the thoughts are not scattered — how could it possibly mean “not practicing various practices together”? Master Ouyi brings this into the clear:
“The one-mind of practice is the bright and distinct, neither drowsy nor scattered.”
(The Collected Treatises of Master Lingfeng
Occasional Talks in the Brahma Chamber)
As for what “one-mind” is, Master Tanluan, in his Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, teaches clearly:
“One-mind means thought following thought in continuity, with no other thought mixed in between.”
(See
Master Tanluan’s Teachings on the Pure Land
for the full text.)
And these people
say: “Master Shandao has a gāthā that explains one-mind undisturbed, saying:

‘The Land of Bliss, nirvāṇa’s unconditioned state, / With mixed and scattered good, few reach it and but wait; / So the Tathāgata chose the essential Dharma bright, / To chant Amitabha, single-minded day and night.’

” Thereupon they conclude: “'One-mind' means concentrated attention, and 'not-scattered' means not mixing — not mixing in the practice of various other methods. So, quite simply, 'one-mind undisturbed' just means 'single-minded.'”“'One-mind undisturbed' is 'single-minded, repeated,'
not mixing with the practice of various other methods

In fact, Master Shandao’s gāthā “To chant Amitabha, single-minded and repeated” teaches us to hold fast exclusively to the name, and to let deluded thoughts grow fewer and fewer — single-minded, repeated. Then to what degree of singleness must one come before rebirth is attained? Master Shandao teaches clearly:

“If one is continuous, one is reborn. If one can keep thought following thought in continuity, taking the end of life as the limit, then of ten, ten will be reborn; of a hundred, a hundred will be reborn.”
Then he exhorts in all earnestness:

“May all beings reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and master oneself, not letting up day or night. When the former thought ends this life, the very next thought is born there, forever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, even unto Buddhahood — is this not most blissful!”
(See
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teachings

for the full text.) And thought following thought in continuity is precisely what Master Ouyi calls “the bright and distinct, neither drowsy nor scattered,” and precisely what Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta calls “gathering in the six sense faculties with pure thoughts succeeding one another”
— this is the correct interpretation of “one-mind undisturbed.”
We

distinguish the meaning of the sūtras in order to guide our practice, and whether our practice is correct and diligent determines where we will go after death and what we will encounter (the circumstances and experiences).
This is not a contest of words; in the end it will all be settled in reality.

Therefore, when distinguishing the meaning of the sūtras, one must be honest — never deceiving oneself or others — and careful. Otherwise, to have misled only oneself would already be pitiable enough, and still one would mislead so many other people who recite the Buddha’s name. How could one bear the weight of such karmic consequence!

In Chan there is a public case, “When, in the Room of Nirvāṇa, the single lamp shines alone, verify it for yourself,” that is deeply thought-provoking: Master Keqin (the teacher of Master Dahui) was in his youth broadly learned in the scriptures and teachings, and placed himself beneath the seat of the Fifth Ancestor Fayan. One day, entering the room to seek instruction, Keqin gave free rein to his brilliant, contentious eloquence. The Fifth Ancestor, displeased, said:
“Is this enough to overcome birth and death
(can all this rhetoric of yours withstand birth and death?)
? When, in the Room of Nirvāṇa, the single lamp shines alone, verify it for yourself
(when the hour of danger comes, you must verify it yourself)

Master Keqin left in anger. He reached Jinshan and fell gravely ill. In the midst of his peril, he applied all the learning of his life, but nothing proved able to help. Recalling the Fifth Ancestor’s words, he vowed to himself: “As soon as I recover, I will return to the Fifth Ancestor.” Later, once somewhat recovered, he bundled up his things and returned. The Fifth Ancestor, seeing him, was delighted and had him enter the attendants’ quarters.
[The Room of Nirvāṇa] The place where a sick monk is sent to pass away.

Question: As for how one can be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, opinions are many and confused, and students of the Dharma do not know which to follow. How should one discern? How should one decide?

Answer: Choosing the path of practice correctly is a matter of the greatest importance. If the road is chosen wrongly, one’s cart heads north while the destination lies south (nán yuán běi zhé); although one toils diligently, the more one cultivates the more deluded one becomes, afflictions rise in profusion, a whole life is thrown away to no purpose, and after death one falls into the evil realms — how utterly unjust! I urge you to read carefully
Direct Pointing to the West, (see
The Annotated Commentary on Direct Pointing to the West
for the full text)

, which is a record of the teachings of Bodhisattva Jueming Miaoxing from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The title “Direct Pointing to the West” means: to point out precisely the proper path of practice for rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[Heading south while driving north] The destination is in the south, yet the cart is driven north. A metaphor for when one’s action runs exactly contrary to one’s aim.
Question: Why is the Pure Land method called the easy path?

Answer: There are two kinds of paths by which one escapes the cycle of birth and death: the common path and the Pure Land path. The common path requires completely eradicating all afflictions before one can escape the cycle of birth and death — this is extremely difficult. The Pure Land path, by contrast, requires only attaining one-mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation (using the Buddha’s name to subdue the afflictions), and at the hour of death one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, thereby escaping the cycle of birth and death. This is far, far easier than cutting off the afflictions of false views and wrong thinking. Moreover, so long as the method is correct, through earnest, diligent effort one-mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation is attainable by everyone. Hence it is said that the Pure Land method is the easy path.
Question: How can one attain one-mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation?
Answer: The greatest obstacle to attaining one-mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation is deluded thoughts. In the practical training text of the “Thus-As-Explained Practice Online Buddhist Academy,”
Awareness Buddha-Recitation

, the causes of deluded thoughts and how to overcome them effectively are analyzed in detail; and the concrete steps and methods of practice by which one attains one-mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation are explained in detail. As long as one has genuine faith and earnest vows, works hard, advances step by step, and perseveres, one will certainly attain one-mind undisturbed in Buddha-recitation. (For a more specific answer, see
How to Attain One-Mind Undisturbed in Buddha-Recitation
